articles.title: Why an LLM Price Table Needs Provenance, Not Just Numbers
articles.excerpt: Comparing LLM APIs looks simple until the first spreadsheet update. A provider changes one rate, a router lists the same model under a different identifier, and a cached-input discount applies only to…
articles.body: Comparing LLM APIs looks simple until the first spreadsheet update. A provider changes one rate, a router lists the same model under a different identifier, and a cached-input discount applies only to one channel. A single “price per million tokens” column cannot preserve those distinctions. I treat an LLM pricing table as a small provenance system. Every displayed number should answer four questions: which model, which channel, which token type, and which source snapshot produced it. Keep provider and router prices separate The same model can be purchased directly from its provider or through a routing platform. Those routes may have different input and output prices, cache rules, fees, model identifiers, and update times.

articles.excerpt: Every "digital nomad banking guide" on the internet was written by someone who spent three weeks in Bali, used their home country debit card the whole time, and called themselves an expert because the…
articles.body: Every "digital nomad banking guide" on the internet was written by someone who spent three weeks in Bali, used their home country debit card the whole time, and called themselves an expert because they "didn't have any problems." Then you actually go nomad. You spend six months hopping between Mexico City, Lisbon, and Chiang Mai. Your home bank flags your card as fraud in Thailand. The ATM in Portugal eats your card. You realize you've paid $847 in foreign transaction fees and ATM surcharges in eight months. Your client pays you via SWIFT and $45 disappears in intermediary bank fees. You owe taxes in a country you've never lived in because you triggered residency rules you didn't know existed. This guide is for the second person.

articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady Mirae is a small Raspberry Pi 5 companion robot I'm designing, and this week I gave it one job that rewards…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built Mirae is a small Raspberry Pi 5 companion robot I'm designing, and this week I gave it one job that rewards being lazy: it tells you one continuing story, a new episode every night. Most AI stories are one-shots. You ask, you get a tale, and by morning it's gone. Mirae tells a series . Every night it writes the next episode of the same story, beginning where the last one ended. A captain introduced on night one is still the captain on night thirty. A stranger who joins on night two is still aboard on night nine. A character who dies stays dead. You never recap, never remind it who is who, never keep notes. Mirae keeps the notebook for you.

articles.title: Why autoscaling a MongoDB replica set by CPU alone breaks consistency — and what we tried instead
articles.excerpt: Scaling a stateless service is easy: add pods when CPU rises, remove them when it falls. A MongoDB replica set doesn't work like that. A secondary that's still catching up on replication isn't really…
articles.body: Scaling a stateless service is easy: add pods when CPU rises, remove them when it falls. A MongoDB replica set doesn't work like that. A secondary that's still catching up on replication isn't really usable capacity yet. Count it anyway, and you think you have headroom you don't. Scale down after a failure, and you can remove a replica before it's safe to do so. That's the problem our paper tackles: consistency-aware autoscaling for stateful microservices under replication lag and failure-recovery constraints. The core idea: count only fresh capacity CAAS, the autoscaler in the paper, runs a MAPE-K loop with four rules that matter more than the loop itself: Lag detection that counts only non-stale secondaries.

articles.body: Se você trabalha com sistemas distribuídos e arquitetura em nuvem , já deve ter se deparado com as falácias da computação distribuída. A rede não é confiável, a latência não é zero e a topologia muda constantemente. Servidores caem, zonas de disponibilidade (AZs) inteiras sofrem instabilidade e bancos de dados entram em deadlock. Historicamente, a engenharia de software tentou construir sistemas perfeitos onde a falha era tratada como uma anomalia inadmissível. Hoje, a abordagem arquitetural mais madura é exatamente o oposto: nós abraçamos a falha. Desenvolvemos com a premissa de que a degradação de componentes é inevitável. É aqui que entra o Chaos Engineering .

articles.title: MVP — Minimum Viable Person: a survival tracker that knows how long you'll survive
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady Two buttons. That's the whole app. MVP — Minimum Viable Person is a survival tracker that knows how long you…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady Two buttons. That's the whole app. MVP — Minimum Viable Person is a survival tracker that knows how long you'll survive. Tap ATE when you eat, tap DRANK when you drink. The app converts each into survival hours using the pop-science "rule of threes" (~3 days without water, ~3 weeks without food). Two tanks — food and water — drain in real time, counting down every second. When they run low, a notification nags you, the buttons pulse, and a lazy AI roommate comments on your continued existence. It rewards laziness twice over: the tracking costs one tap, and everything the AI writes assumes you won't try.

articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.body: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's a still image, video, audio, or text - that "has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence" to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies , as well as restaurants' ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
